indicators.note: 'say' asks us to speak the earth's other name and hear a different spelling

blocks.note: the globe we live on, spoken out loud

explanation.surface: A record of someone sailing or flying all the way round the globe.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that whirled spun or turned round and round, which is going in circles.

blocks.note: first meaning: gone wrong, out of control
second meaning: farm wire used to tie bales

explanation.surface: A muddled country bookbinder.
explanation.walkthrough: The informal sense of chaos comes from tangled baling wire on farms.
explanation.definitionFit: Going crazy or erratic is an idiom, and literally it is wire used to bind bales on a farm.

clue.text: Condition under which a horse races

definitions.note: a descriptive phrase for the jockey on top

blocks.note: first meaning: a clause added to a document
second meaning: the person on the horse's back

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests the going or the ground; but what a horse races under is the jockey on its back.
explanation.definitionFit: An added clause or proviso to a contract, and the jockey sitting astride a horse.

blocks.note: first meaning: revealed or uncovered
second meaning: unprotected, open to attack

explanation.definitionFit: Something revealed to view, and something left unprotected and open to harm.

blocks.note: surface reading: tears rising in the eyes
setter's reading: a tint or blush spreading up through something

explanation.surface: Emotion rising, perhaps tears welling up or a face flushing.
explanation.definitionFit: To spread gradually over or through something, especially a colour or light, as a blush spreads across cheeks.

indicators.note: letters moving freely are not fixed in place, so they can be rearranged

blocks.note: U is the abbreviation for university
taken as written

explanation.surface: Advice to a student to go to college and splash out.
explanation.definitionFit: To tip something is to turn it over or set it on end, as when a crate is turned upside down.

clue.text: US rifle is adapted for infantrymen

indicators.note: something adapted has been modified, so the letters are put in a fresh order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An American gun being modified for use by foot soldiers.
explanation.definitionFit: Soldiers in regiments originally armed with light muskets, now the name of several British infantry regiments.

clue.text: They will run away when things warm up

definitions.text: They will run away when things warm up

blocks.clueFragment: They will run away when things warm up
blocks.note: surface reading: cowards who flee when a fight gets heated

blocks.clueFragment: They will run away when things warm up
blocks.note: setter's reading: figures that melt and trickle away in a thaw

explanation.surface: Cowards who bolt as soon as the action heats up.
explanation.definitionFit: Figures built from packed snow in winter melt and flow away as water when the weather turns mild.

clue.text: Guard put on health risk in naval vessel

blocks.note: an escort guards whoever it accompanies
a carrier spreads disease without necessarily suffering it

explanation.surface: A sentry being stationed on a ship because of an infection danger.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, 'put on' places the first piece above the second.
explanation.definitionFit: A small aircraft-carrying warship used to protect convoys, especially in the Second World War.

clue.text: US polar explorer - and aviator, by the way

blocks.note: taken as written
RD is the abbreviation for road, a way

explanation.surface: A passing remark that a famous polar explorer also flew aircraft.
explanation.walkthrough: 'by the way' looks like a throwaway aside, but it is the wordplay. Richard Byrd flew over the South Pole in 1929.
explanation.definitionFit: Richard E. Byrd was an American naval officer who pioneered flights over both polar regions.

blocks.note: surface reading: a fiendishly tight grip, as of a ball in a game
setter's reading: a demon taking over someone's body and soul

explanation.surface: Fiendishly strong command, perhaps of a ball or a team.
explanation.definitionFit: Demonic takeover of a person, as in exorcism stories, is called by the same word as ownership or keeping the ball.

blocks.note: surface reading: the royal regalia kept in the Tower of London
setter's reading: jewelled ornaments worn on the crown of the head

explanation.surface: The royal regalia on display in the Tower of London.
explanation.definitionFit: These jewelled semicircular headbands are worn on top of the head, the crown, by royalty and brides.

blocks.note: surface reading: a fondness for history or nostalgia
setter's reading: a person one once loved, a former sweetheart

explanation.surface: A nostalgic fondness for history and bygone times.
explanation.definitionFit: A former sweetheart or partner is a person once loved, now in one's romantic history.

blocks.note: surface reading: a bill settled after its due date
setter's reading: tax paid on behalf of someone deceased, 'late' meaning dead

explanation.surface: An overdue bill settled after the deadline.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Late' as in 'the late Mr Smith' means dead. This was the British tax on estates, now called inheritance tax.
explanation.definitionFit: A tax levied on an estate when its owner dies is money owed because someone has passed away.

clue.text: A cleaner at work among the chatterers

definitions.text: A cleaner at work among the chatterers

blocks.clueFragment: A cleaner at work among the chatterers
blocks.note: surface reading: an office cleaner surrounded by gossiping staff

blocks.clueFragment: A cleaner at work among the chatterers
blocks.note: setter's reading: 'chatterers' are teeth, which chatter in the cold

explanation.surface: A cleaner doing the rounds among gossiping colleagues.
explanation.definitionFit: A small pointed stick used to remove food lodged between the teeth after a meal.

blocks.note: first meaning: a female donkey or wren
second meaning: the spinning machine of the early Industrial Revolution

explanation.surface: A woman working at a mill spinning cotton.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one woman mill worker; the clue is two separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names a she-ass or hen wren, and Hargreaves's multi-spindle spinning machine.

definitions.note: a verb phrase standing for the adjective: one who is aglow looks healthy

blocks.note: Ag is the chemical symbol for silver
feeling down means feeling low

explanation.surface: Someone with grey hair who feels depressed but still has a good complexion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Silver' and 'down' suggest a grey-haired, gloomy person, but they are separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Glowing with warmth and colour, as rosy cheeks show good health and vitality.

blocks.note: surface reading: an English narrowboat on an inland waterway
setter's reading: the oared boat of Venice's waterways

explanation.surface: A boat on a canal, of the sort seen on British waterways.
explanation.definitionFit: The flat-bottomed Venetian boat propelled by a standing oarsman plies the city's canals.

blocks.note: surface reading: someone employed to clean a pub
setter's reading: the Rovers Return is the pub, a bar, in Coronation Street, a soap opera

explanation.surface: A charwoman who cleans the famous pub in a TV soap.
explanation.walkthrough: Coronation Street is Britain's longest-running TV soap opera, and the Rovers Return is its pub; so its bar is a bar in a soap, and a cake of soap cleans.
explanation.definitionFit: A cake of soap is something that cleans, and the punning reading gives a pub bar in a soap opera.

blocks.note: an individual is one person
eyed means looked at

explanation.surface: A single onlooker watching the giant of Greek myth.
explanation.walkthrough: Polyphemus is the Cyclops blinded by Odysseus in the Odyssey.
explanation.definitionFit: Polyphemus was a Cyclops, a giant with a single eye in the middle of his forehead.

clue.text: Not a sum that's incorrect - sums

indicators.note: an incorrect version has gone wrong, so its letters are jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A teacher marking arithmetic, saying a wrong sum is no sum at all.
explanation.definitionFit: Totals or quantities of money are sums, and the plural noun matches the plural definition.

clue.text: Defame a large number and get into a row

blocks.note: M is the Roman numeral for a thousand
to align things is to put them in line

explanation.surface: Slandering lots of people and starting a quarrel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'row' wants to be a quarrel, which fits the slander; here it is a line.
explanation.definitionFit: To speak harmful untruths about someone, damaging their reputation.

clue.text: It's unusual to hear in broadcasting

indicators.note: an unusual arrangement is one out of the ordinary, so the letters are reordered

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A remark that it is rare to hear something on radio or television.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to hear' and 'broadcasting' share a radio theme, which hides that the fodder runs on through 'in'.
explanation.definitionFit: A programme being transmitted live by radio or television is said to be going out right now.

clue.text: In school, put us at the end of the line

indicators.note: putting something in a place means it sits inside that place

blocks.note: Eton is the famous English public school
taken as written

explanation.surface: Pupils complaining that they are put at the back of the queue.
explanation.walkthrough: Euston is a major London railway terminus, where trains from the north-west end their run.
explanation.definitionFit: A terminus station is literally where a railway line ends, and this one is in London.

clue.text: It's bound to be a bit of a shock

definitions.text: It's bound to be a bit of a shock

blocks.clueFragment: It's bound to be a bit of a shock
blocks.note: surface reading: something certain to come as a surprise

blocks.clueFragment: It's bound to be a bit of a shock
blocks.note: setter's reading: a tied bundle forming part of a stook of corn in a field

explanation.surface: A warning that something is certain to surprise.
explanation.walkthrough: A shock is an old word for a stook: bundles of cut corn stood up together in a field to dry.
explanation.definitionFit: A bundle of cut cereal stalks tied together, several of which stand up together in the field.

indicators.note: something misguided has gone astray, so these letters are set in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A rueful remark that misplaced affection is truly just compassion.
explanation.definitionFit: Both adverbs work as intensifiers meaning truly or absolutely, as in 'it was really awful'.

blocks.note: surface reading: a racehorse that is the hot favourite
setter's reading: a mountain with a hot top from which lava may flow

explanation.surface: A racing tip about a horse fancied to win.
explanation.walkthrough: A jockey's horse is his mount and a hot tip is a favourite; but here the mount is a mountain whose tip is hot.
explanation.definitionFit: Sicily's active volcano has a fiery summit, and its molten lava flows down the slopes.

blocks.note: surface reading: hangers-on of a woman called Hazel
setter's reading: the dangling flower spikes of the hazel tree

explanation.surface: The sycophants clinging to a woman named Hazel.
explanation.definitionFit: Hazel trees bear dangling flower clusters in late winter, which hang from the twigs.

blocks.note: odd means unusual
to angle is to fish

explanation.surface: A strange viewpoint attributed to an eccentric person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'angle' looks like a noun, a point of view, but it is the verb for fishing with rod and line.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are informal terms for an eccentric person whose behaviour is peculiar.
